Note the tests must all run in PARALLEL, which is exactly why the 24-hour constraint is in the question - sequential testing would allow a different trade-off. The general technique is what to take away: whenever a puzzle asks for the minimum number of tests, weighings or questions, count the information. Each outcome with m possible results gives log2(m) bits, and you need at least log2(number of cases) bits in total. That single argument gives the 10 here, gives log3 for balance-scale weighing problems where each weighing has three outcomes, and gives the n log n lower bound for comparison sorting.
questions.technique: Information-theoretic lower bound via bit counting
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the bound is easy once framed as bits, and the binary-labelling construction confirms it.

questions.prompt: How do you test whether a positive integer n is a power of two in constant time?
options: Check that n & (n - 1) equals 0
Check that n % 2 equals 0
Repeatedly divide by 2 and check for a remainder
Check that log2(n) is an integer
questions.explanation: n & (n-1) == 0. A power of two has exactly one set bit; subtracting 1 flips that bit to 0 and sets all the lower bits to 1, so the AND is zero. For anything else, the highest set bit survives the AND and the result is non-zero. One operation, constant time. Checking n % 2 == 0 only tests evenness, so 6 would pass. Repeated division works but is O(log n) rather than constant. The floating-point log test is the dangerous one: it looks fine and fails on large values because log2 of a big integer is not exactly representable, so log2(2^49) can come out as 48.99999999999999. That is a real bug class, and saying so is worth as much as the correct answer. The related idiom n & (n-1) also clears the lowest set bit, which gives Brian Kernighan's population-count loop.
questions.technique: Bit manipulation for powers of two
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: a single idiom, though the floating-point distractor is a genuine trap.

questions.prompt: Monte Carlo error falls as 1/sqrt(N). Given that, why is Monte Carlo the standard tool for high-dimensional option pricing, and how would you speed it up without simply running more paths?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because the 1/sqrt(N) rate is INDEPENDENT of dimension, while grid methods degrade exponentially with it. To speed it up, reduce variance rather than increase N: antithetic variates, control variates, importance sampling for rare events, and quasi-random (low-discrepancy) sequences.
questions.explanation: Why it wins in high dimensions: a grid or lattice method with m points per dimension needs m^d points in d dimensions, so accuracy collapses exponentially as d grows - the curse of dimensionality. Monte Carlo's error is c/sqrt(N) where the constant c depends on the payoff's variance but NOT on d. So there is a crossover dimension, typically around 3 or 4, beyond which Monte Carlo simply wins. A basket option on 30 names is a 30-dimensional integral, and nothing else is practical. How to speed it up. Note first that halving the error by brute force requires FOUR times the paths, so variance reduction is where the leverage is. (1) ANTITHETIC VARIATES: for every path driven by Z, also run the path driven by -Z and average. Costs nothing extra in random numbers and reduces variance whenever the payoff is monotonic in Z, because the two estimates are negatively correlated. (2) CONTROL VARIATES: simulate alongside a related quantity whose exact value you know - price an Asian option using the geometric-average Asian, which has a closed form, and correct by the known error. This is usually the biggest win available, often an order of magnitude. (3) IMPORTANCE SAMPLING: for rare events such as deep out-of-the-money options or credit tail losses, sample from a shifted distribution that visits the important region often, then reweight. Without it, most paths contribute zero and the estimator is nearly useless. (4) QUASI-MONTE CARLO: replace pseudo-random numbers with a low-discrepancy sequence (Sobol, Halton), which fills space more evenly and can achieve close to 1/N in moderate dimensions - though the advantage degrades in very high dimensions and error estimates become harder. (5) Mundane but real: use common random numbers when comparing scenarios so the differences are not swamped by simulation noise.
questions.technique: Why the dimension-free rate matters, and variance reduction
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the dimension argument is the key insight; naming concrete variance-reduction methods is the depth.

questions.prompt: In a finite-difference PDE solver for option pricing, what is the main trade-off between the explicit and implicit schemes?
options: Explicit is simple but only conditionally stable, needing a time step of order (space step) squared; implicit is unconditionally stable but must solve a linear system each step
Explicit is more accurate but slower
Implicit only works for European options
Explicit requires a uniform grid while implicit does not
questions.explanation: The explicit scheme computes each new value directly from known neighbours - trivial to code, no linear algebra - but it is only CONDITIONALLY stable, requiring roughly dt <= (dx)^2/(sigma^2 S^2). Halving the space step forces you to quarter the time step, so refining the grid becomes brutally expensive. The implicit scheme expresses each new value in terms of unknown neighbours, so every step requires solving a tridiagonal system, but it is unconditionally stable and you can take whatever time step accuracy demands. Crank-Nicolson averages the two: second-order accurate in time as well as space, still unconditionally stable, and the usual default. Its known weakness is worth mentioning - it can produce spurious oscillations near a discontinuous payoff such as a digital option, and the standard fix is Rannacher smoothing, taking a few fully implicit steps first. Also worth noting that the explicit scheme is essentially the trinomial tree, and its stability condition is exactly the condition that the implied 'probabilities' stay non-negative.
questions.technique: Stability versus cost in finite-difference schemes
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the stability condition is the substance, and the Crank-Nicolson oscillation caveat is the extension.

questions.prompt: You receive a stream of numbers and must report the running mean at every step, without storing the history. How do you do it, and how would you also track the running variance?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Keep a count and update the mean incrementally: mean_n = mean_(n-1) + (x_n - mean_(n-1))/n. For variance use Welford's algorithm: maintain M2 with M2 += (x_n - mean_old)*(x_n - mean_new), and the variance is M2/(n-1).
questions.explanation: MEAN. The naive approach stores a running sum and divides, which works but loses precision badly for long streams and large values, because the sum grows without bound while the increments do not. The incremental form mean_n = mean_(n-1) + (x_n - mean_(n-1))/n keeps the accumulator at the scale of the data and is numerically far better behaved. VARIANCE. The textbook formula Var = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 is a well-known numerical disaster: when the mean is large relative to the standard deviation, you subtract two nearly equal large numbers and lose most of your significant digits - it can even return a negative variance. Welford's algorithm avoids the cancellation entirely. Maintain n, mean, and M2 (the running sum of squared deviations). For each new x: n += 1; delta = x - mean; mean += delta/n; delta2 = x - mean; M2 += delta*delta2. Then the sample variance is M2/(n-1). One pass, constant memory, numerically stable. Two extensions interviewers often add. For an EXPONENTIALLY WEIGHTED mean, use mean = lambda*mean + (1-lambda)*x, which needs no count at all and is what EWMA volatility estimation does. For a SLIDING WINDOW of fixed size k you do need to store the k values, since you must subtract the departing observation - and that is exactly the rolling-window ghost-feature problem in volatility estimation, where an old large return leaving the window causes a phantom jump.
questions.technique: Numerically stable streaming statistics
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the mean is easy; knowing why the naive variance formula fails is the real content.

questions.prompt: What is the lower bound on the number of comparisons needed to sort n items, and why?
options: Order n log n, because n! outcomes require at least log2(n!) binary comparisons
Order n, because each item must be examined at least once
Order n^2, because every pair must be compared
There is no lower bound; it depends on the algorithm
questions.explanation: Omega(n log n) for COMPARISON-based sorting. The argument is information-theoretic: there are n! possible orderings, each comparison has two outcomes and so yields at most one bit, and distinguishing n! cases requires at least log2(n!) bits. By Stirling, log2(n!) is approximately n*log2(n) - 1.44n, so the bound is Omega(n log n). Merge sort and heap sort achieve it, so it is tight. The crucial qualifier is COMPARISON-based. Algorithms that use the structure of the keys rather than comparing them can beat it: counting sort and radix sort are O(n) or O(nk) for bounded integer keys, because they extract more than one bit per operation by indexing directly. Being able to name that exception is what distinguishes understanding the bound from reciting it - and it is the same bit-counting argument as the poisoned-wine problem, applied to a different outcome space.
questions.technique: Information-theoretic sorting lower bound
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: the argument is short, and the comparison-based qualifier is the point.

questions.prompt: You have a fair coin and need to simulate an event with probability exactly 1/3. How do you do it, and what is the expected number of tosses? Now the reverse: you have a BIASED coin with unknown p and need a fair 50/50 decision.
questions.canonicalAnswer: For 1/3: toss twice, map HH to success, HT and TH to failure, and reject TT and repeat. Expected tosses 8/3. For a fair decision from a biased coin: von Neumann's trick — toss twice, call HT one outcome and TH the other, discard HH and TT.
questions.explanation: SIMULATING 1/3 WITH A FAIR COIN. A fair coin generates powers of 2, and 3 is not one, so no fixed-length scheme can work exactly. Use rejection sampling: toss twice for four equally likely outcomes, assign HH to the 1/3 event, HT and TH to the 2/3 event, and REJECT TT, starting over. Conditional on accepting, the probabilities are exactly 1/3 and 2/3. Expected tosses: each round of 2 tosses is accepted with probability 3/4, so the number of rounds is geometric with mean 4/3 and the expected tosses are 8/3 = 2.67. It terminates with probability 1 despite having no fixed length. A FAIR DECISION FROM A BIASED COIN (von Neumann). Toss twice. HT and TH each have probability p(1-p) - identical, whatever p is - so call HT 'heads' and TH 'tails' and discard HH and TT. The result is exactly fair regardless of the bias, and crucially you never need to know p. Expected tosses: each pair is decisive with probability 2p(1-p), so the expected number of tosses is 1/(p(1-p)), which is 4 for a fair coin and blows up for a very biased one - at p = 0.01 you need about 101 tosses on average. Both answers share one idea worth naming: when you cannot produce the distribution you want directly, produce something you CAN and then condition on an event that restores the symmetry you need. That is rejection sampling, and it is the same principle behind acceptance-rejection methods for sampling arbitrary continuous densities.
questions.technique: Rejection sampling to change a distribution's granularity
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: each half is a known trick, and seeing that both are rejection sampling is the unifying point.
